readings.title: The Island of the Nine Whirlpools, part 1: The witch’s price
readings.challenge: Match each thing the Queen gives up to what it becomes, and notice what the witch wants when she is offered anything at all.
readings.focus: A Queen pays a witch everything she is wearing for a child, then gives the witch the one thing money cannot buy.
readings.context: E. Nesbit (Edith Nesbit, 1858–1924) was an English writer of funny, magical stories for children. The Book of Dragons (1900) collects eight dragon tales. In this one the narrator often talks straight to the reader, calls the reader “my dear,” and jokes about school lessons. An enchanter is a magician; a cauldron is a big cooking pot; sapphires are blue jewels and rubies red ones; clasps are fastenings; wits are cleverness; a curtsy is a little bow made by bending the knees; to be civil is to be polite. “As much as your place is worth” means you would be in big trouble.

excerpt.locator: V. “The Island of the Nine Whirlpools,” from the beginning to the Queen going home past the snakes; opens “The dark arch that led to the witch's cave was hung with a black-and-yellow fringe of…”; closes “…was friends with their mistress; so, of course, they had to do their best to be civil.”.

questions.prompt: The witch warns that a child will bring sorrow. How does the Queen answer each warning, and what does this show about her?
facilitatorNotes: She says “It will bring me joy first” and then “Greater joy”: she believes the joy will be worth the sorrow. She is brave and determined. Ask readers to keep the warning in mind as the story goes on.
evidence: Do you know it will bring you sorrow?
It will bring me joy first,

questions.prompt: What does the witch take from the Queen? What does each thing become in the child?
facilitatorNotes: The gold crown becomes golden hair; the sapphires blue eyes; the rubies red lips; the pearls clear, pale skin; the lilies a white, sweet soul; the diamonds clear wits.
evidence: Your child will have hair as golden as your crown, eyes as blue as your sapphires.
Its soul will be white and sweet as your lilies, and your diamonds will be no clearer than its wits.

questions.prompt: The Queen offers a country or a sack of jewels. What does the witch want instead, and how does the Queen give it to her?
facilitatorNotes: Someone to love her. The Queen throws her arms round her neck, kisses her half a hundred times, and says the baby shall love her too.
evidence: I should like some one to love me,
Then the Queen threw her arms around the witch's neck and kissed her half a hundred times.

questions.prompt: Most fairy-tale witches are wicked. Is this one? Use what she says and does.
facilitatorNotes: She lives behind snakes and asks a price, but she wants nothing for herself, longs to be loved, and promises to come when sorrow comes. Even her snakes try to curtsy once the Queen is her friend. Most readers will say she is kind; some may still find her frightening.
evidence: I could make more diamonds in a day than I should wear in a year.
Each of your fifty kisses will be a spell to bring me to you.

readings.title: The Island of the Nine Whirlpools, part 2: The Lone Tower
readings.challenge: Watch the King’s temper, and decide what he is really punishing the Princess for.
readings.focus: Angry that his child is a girl, the enchanter-King shuts his daughter on an island no one can reach.
readings.context: Recap: a Queen, whose husband is a King and an enchanter, visited a kind witch to ask for a baby. She gave the witch her crown, her jewels, her lilies and fifty kisses. The witch warned that the child would bring great sorrow, and promised to come if the Queen called. The Royal arms are a royal family’s badge; blazoned means painted; an heir is the one who will rule next; a laboratory is a room for experiments, and crucibles are pots for melting things in; a dowry is money given with a bride; an income is money paid to you regularly; a griffin is a creature that is half eagle and half lion.
readings.contentNote: The King is furious that his baby is a girl, because he wanted a son to inherit his kingdom and his magic; the story shows him as wrong and unkind.

excerpt.locator: V. “The Island of the Nine Whirlpools,” from the Queen finding the baby at home to the Princess left on the island; opens “When the Queen got home, sure enough there was the baby lying in the cradle with the…”; closes “…Princess was left, with the dragon and the griffin, on the Island of the Nine Whirlpools.”.

questions.prompt: Why is the King furious when he sees the baby? Whom does he blame?
facilitatorNotes: He wanted a boy, an heir and Prince, to learn his magic and rule after him. He blames the Queen for asking only for “a child.” Ask whether that was really anyone’s fault.
evidence: a boy, an heir, a Prince
And the Queen hung her head and had to confess that she had only asked for a child.

questions.prompt: On her eighteenth birthday, what does the Princess say to her father? Why does she speak out now?
facilitatorNotes: “You oughtn't to speak to my mother like that.” She suddenly feels grown up. Her mother, frightened, tells her not to interfere.
evidence: You oughtn't to speak to my mother like that,
it came to her suddenly and all in a moment that she was a grown-up, so she spoke out.

questions.prompt: What must the man who marries the Princess be able to do? Why does the King make it so hard?
facilitatorNotes: Sail through the Nine Whirlpools and kill the dragon and the griffin. He says he will “teach her to respect her father”; really he is getting back at her for standing up to him, and at the Queen.
evidence: He'll have to be clever enough to sail a ship through the Nine Whirlpools that spin around the island, and to kill the dragon and the griffin.
I'm only going to teach her to respect her father.

questions.prompt: The King calls her “my dear, respectful daughter” and “my dutiful child.” Does he mean it? What does that show about him?
facilitatorNotes: No: he says the opposite of what he means, to mock her for speaking up. He gives her money and servants so it sounds generous, but it is a prison. Readers may connect this to the witch’s warning of sorrow.
evidence: Here you shall stay, my dear, respectful daughter, till the clever man comes to marry you.
I wish you joy, my dutiful child.

readings.title: The Island of the Nine Whirlpools, part 3: Two stone ladies
readings.challenge: Notice what the Queen and the witch each give up, and how quickly the story jumps across hundreds of years.
readings.focus: The Queen and the witch turn to stone beside the Princess, and long afterwards a sailor-boy sees a light at sea.
readings.context: Recap: an enchanter-King, angry that his only child was a girl, shut the Princess in the Lone Tower on an island ringed by the Nine Whirlpools, guarded by a dragon and a griffin, until a man clever enough to pass them comes to marry her. Her mother, the Queen, had got her baby from a kind witch, giving her fifty kisses, and the witch promised to come when sorrow came. A scepter is a rod a ruler holds; a tablet is a flat stone with writing on it; to be delivered is to be rescued, and the deliverer is the rescuer. “’Bout ship!” means turn the ship round; discreetly means quietly and sensibly. Scores are twenties; a skipper is a ship’s captain; to reef a sail is to roll part of it up; a chart is a map of the sea.
readings.contentNote: Many princes drown in the whirlpools trying to reach the Princess.

excerpt.locator: V. “The Island of the Nine Whirlpools,” from the Queen calling the witch to the skipper’s warning about the light of the Lone Tower; opens “The Queen, left at home, cried for a day and a night, and then she remembered the witch…”; closes “…more of the Princess, for that is only an idle tale. But the whirlpools are quite real."”.

questions.prompt: What must the Queen become to be with her daughter? What is her answer?
facilitatorNotes: She must be turned to stone until the spell is lifted. She says she would be a stone for a thousand years if she could see her daughter again at the end.
evidence: you will have to be turned to stone, and to stay so till the spell is taken off the child.
I would be a stone for a thousand years,

questions.prompt: What does the witch give up to help? What will she be if they ever come out of the stone?
facilitatorNotes: All her witch’s powers; she will be “only a happy old woman.” She does it for the Queen’s fifty kisses: the love she wanted in part 1.
evidence: In doing this for you I lose all my witch's powers,
I shall be a witch no more, but only a happy old woman.

questions.prompt: Many princes came for the Princess. What happened to them? What does the narrator think of the ones who turned back?
facilitatorNotes: Some went down in the whirlpools; others looked, said “’Bout ship!” and sailed home. The narrator teases them: their heads are “wise,” their kingdoms “nice, safe, comfortable.” Readers can decide whether turning back was sensible or cowardly.
evidence: roaring in triumph the story of many a good ship that had gone down in their swirl,
gone discreetly home to their nice, safe, comfortable kingdoms.

questions.prompt: The skipper tells Nigel never to steer toward the light. What do you predict Nigel will do? What does the “Something” that whispers to him have to do with it?
facilitatorNotes: Most readers will predict he goes, because the Something that knows who is “worthy to be Princes” has chosen him, and because being told “think no more of the Princess” makes him think of nothing else.
evidence: And this Something came from the farther side of the seventh world, and whispered in the boy's ear.
and think no more of the Princess, for that is only an idle tale.

readings.title: The Island of the Nine Whirlpools, part 4: Five minutes a day
readings.challenge: Follow how patient watching finds a way in, and spot the new problem Nigel has to solve.
readings.focus: By watching for seven days, Nigel finds the five minutes when he can reach the island, and meets the Princess.
readings.context: Recap: long ago an enchanter-King shut his daughter, the Princess, in the Lone Tower on an island ringed by the Nine Whirlpools and guarded by a dragon and a griffin; her mother the Queen and a kind witch stand at the gate, turned to stone, to be near her. Hundreds of years later a sailor-boy called Nigel saw the tower’s light, and his uncle the skipper warned him never to go near. Primrose is pale yellow; the first declension is an early Latin lesson; the Norman Kings ruled England after 1066; a chronometer is a very exact ship’s clock; to beach a boat is to pull it up on the shore.

excerpt.locator: V. “The Island of the Nine Whirlpools,” from Nigel taking the ship’s boat to the Princess leaving him to his arithmetic; opens “So, of course, from that day Nigel thought of nothing else. And as he sailed hither and…”; closes “…Be a good boy, and get your sum done." And she ran away and left him to his arithmetic.”.

questions.prompt: How does Nigel find a way through the whirlpools? Why does the narrator say seven days of watching is enough?
facilitatorNotes: He watches until he learns that for five minutes a day the whirlpools stop and the tide goes out, five minutes earlier each day. She says anyone who gives seven days’ whole thought to something will learn it, even the nine-times table.
evidence: For you are certain to know something if you give for seven days your whole thought to it,
for five minutes out of the 1,440 minutes that make up a day the whirlpools slipped into silence,

questions.prompt: When Nigel says he can kill the dragon and the griffin, what does the Princess answer? Who sounds more grown up?
facilitatorNotes: “Don't be a silly boy”: he has no sword or shield. She is “pretending to be very grown up”; she has been on the island for ages but is still eighteen. Readers can decide who is wiser here.
evidence: said the Princess, pretending to be very grown up,
You haven't a sword, or a shield, or anything!

questions.prompt: What does the Princess tell him about when the dragon sleeps? Why does Nigel then ask, “can you do sums?”
facilitatorNotes: The dragon sleeps (and turns to stone) for five minutes a day, three minutes later each day. The low tide comes five minutes earlier each day, so Nigel must work out when the two will come together.
evidence: but the dragon sleeps every day for five minutes, and every day it is three minutes later than it was the day before.
can you do sums?

questions.prompt: The Princess says she does not know what Time is. How does she spend her days on the island? Would you like to live like that?
facilitatorNotes: She sews flowers on her golden wedding gown; the griffin does the housework and the dragon the cooking. The witch’s spell makes all days like one day, so she never grows sad or older. Some readers will envy her; others will find it lonely or empty.
evidence: but I don't know what Time is.
And the dragon does the cooking

readings.title: The Island of the Nine Whirlpools, part 5: Love and Arithmetic
readings.challenge: Enjoy the joke about school maths, then follow the plan as it unfolds.
readings.focus: The answer to Nigel’s sum was waiting on a statue all along, and he uses it to lead the dragon to the sea.
readings.context: Recap: long ago an enchanter-King shut the Princess in the Lone Tower on an island ringed by the Nine Whirlpools, guarded by a dragon and a griffin; her mother and a kind witch stand at the gate, turned to stone, the witch holding a tablet with words on it. A sailor-boy, Nigel, found that the whirlpools stop for five minutes a day, five minutes earlier each day, and rowed in to meet the Princess. The dragon falls asleep and turns to stone for five minutes a day, three minutes later each day, and Nigel must work out when the two will come together. Nesbit lists real kinds of school maths (decimals, square roots, algebra, logarithms and more) with a made-up one, “rule-of-three-and-three-quarters”; using them all on one small sum is the joke. A magnolia is a tree with big, smooth leaves; Cannon Street Station is a railway station in London; bayonets are blades fixed to rifles.
readings.contentNote: The dragon breathes fire as he chases Nigel.

excerpt.locator: V. “The Island of the Nine Whirlpools,” from Nigel’s sum to the dragon chasing him across the sand; opens “Now, the sum was this: "If the whirlpools stop and the tide goes down once in every…”; closes “…dragon after him. And the tide was low, and sleepy little waves lapped the sand's edge.”.

questions.prompt: The narrator calls it “quite a simple sum” that “You could do it in a minute.” Does she mean it? Why does Nigel get a different answer every time?
facilitatorNotes: She is teasing: it is a tricky problem, and Nigel throws every method he knows at it, so he gets a new answer each time and cannot tell which is right. Readers may know the feeling.
evidence: It is quite a simple sum, as you see:
He got an answer every time, it is true, but it was always a different one,

questions.prompt: Where does the answer come from? What do you think T and D stand for, and what might the last line be a clue to?
facilitatorNotes: From the stone tablet the witch-statue holds; the Princess copies it on a magnolia leaf. T is the tide and D the dragon. “The griffin is artificial” is a clue for later. Readers can guess what R means (perhaps “right”).
evidence: this is what is written on the tablet of the statue by the lower gate.
P.S.—And the griffin is artificial.

questions.prompt: Nigel says “two great powers are on our side.” What are they? Do you agree they are the strongest in the world?
facilitatorNotes: Love and Arithmetic. Love brought him here; arithmetic found the right moment. Readers can argue for either, or name another power.
evidence: the power of Love and the power of Arithmetic.

questions.prompt: Why does Nigel kiss the Princess in full sight of the dragon? What are the cord and the chronometer for? Predict what happens next.
facilitatorNotes: To make the dragon rage and chase him to the water just as it is about to fall asleep. The Princess watches the clock so she knows when to pull him back with the cord. Readers predict whether the plan works.
evidence: in full sight of the terrace where the dragon kept watch, Nigel took his Princess in his arms and kissed her.
so as to know when to pull the rope.

readings.title: The Island of the Nine Whirlpools, part 6: As long as was good for them
readings.challenge: See how each guardian is beaten by what it is made of, and catch the narrator’s last jokes.
readings.focus: The dragon sleeps and drowns, the griffin fights itself, the stone ladies wake, and the wicked King’s blood is found at last.
readings.context: Recap: long ago an enchanter-King shut his daughter, the Princess, in the Lone Tower on an island ringed by the Nine Whirlpools, guarded by a dragon and a griffin; her mother the Queen and a kind witch turned to stone at the gate to be near her. A sailor-boy, Nigel, reached the island at low tide and, with a clue from the witch-statue’s tablet, worked out the day the tide would go out just before the dragon fell asleep. Now he has kissed the Princess in front of the dragon and run to the sea with the dragon after him, while the Princess holds a cord tied to his arm. A griffin is half eagle and half lion; in an old rhyme the Kilkenny cats fought until only their tails were left. A pedestal is a statue’s stand. “Plowed” was student slang at Oxford University for failing an exam, so the field is plowed like a student. An income is money paid to you regularly.
readings.contentNote: The dragon drowns, and the two halves of the griffin fight each other to death.

excerpt.locator: V. “The Island of the Nine Whirlpools,” from Nigel pausing at the water’s edge to the end of the story; opens “Now at the lip of the water, Nigel paused and looked back, and the dragon made a bound,…”; closes “…on her income—and that is a thing that a great many people would like to be able to do.”.

questions.prompt: How is the dragon beaten? Does Nigel have to fight it?
facilitatorNotes: No: it falls asleep and turns to stone near the water just as the whirlpools return, and drowns, while the Princess pulls Nigel out with the cord. Arithmetic, not a sword, wins.
evidence: But before it reached the shore sleep caught it and turned it to stone.
when he woke up from being asleep he found he was drowned, so there was an end of him.

questions.prompt: How do Nigel and the Princess beat the griffin? Why does their trick work?
facilitatorNotes: Nigel treads on its tail while it sleeps and the Princess cries that a lion is behind it. The King made it from two halves that never got used to each other, so, half asleep, the eagle end and the lion end fight each other.
evidence: Look out! There's a lion behind you.
the two halves had never really got used to each other.

questions.prompt: What made the whirlpools? How does the wicked King’s blood end up doing some good?
facilitatorNotes: Nine drops of his blood, so wicked the sea kept trying to get rid of them. They become nine rubies; thrown on a field, they make the land turn itself over, plowing it.
evidence: Those whirlpools were made by the enchanter-King's dropping nine drops of his blood into the sea.
So the wicked King did some good after all.

questions.prompt: The griffin is buried under the herb-bed because “it wasn't its fault.” Whose fault was it? Thinking back to the witch’s warning, did the child bring sorrow and then greater joy?
facilitatorNotes: The King’s, who made it badly and set it to guard a lady from her lover. The sorrow came with the tower and the stone; the joy came at the end, when everyone “lived happily as long as was good for them.” Readers can say whether the joy was worth the long wait.
evidence: it wasn't its fault that it had been made so badly and put to such poor work as guarding a lady from her lover.
and they all lived happily as long as was good for them.

readings.title: Kind Little Edmund, part 1: An inquiring mind
readings.challenge: Notice when the narrator says one thing and means another.
readings.focus: A boy who wants to find things out, not learn them, goes looking for the source of the noises in the mountain.
readings.context: E. Nesbit (Edith Nesbit, 1858–1924) was an English writer of funny, magical stories for children. The Book of Dragons (1900) collects eight dragon tales. In this one the narrator talks straight to the reader and often says the opposite of what she means: listen for the jokes. To play truant is to skip school; ciphering is arithmetic; Mr. Smiles’s “Self-Help” was a serious Victorian book about improving yourself; stalactites and stalagmites are stony spikes that hang from cave roofs and rise from cave floors.
readings.contentNote: Edmund is caned (hit with a stick) by his schoolmaster, a common school punishment in Nesbit’s time.

excerpt.locator: VIII. “Kind Little Edmund, or The Caves and the Cockatrice,” from the beginning to the three noises in the cave; opens “Edmund was a boy. The people who did not like him said that he was the most tiresome boy…”; closes “…clucking sound, such as a chicken might make if it happened to be as big as a haystack.”.

questions.prompt: What is the difference, for Edmund, between learning things and finding things out? Give an example of each.
facilitatorNotes: Learning is what school teaches, “what everybody knows.” Finding out is taking clocks and locks apart, cutting open a rubber ball, or burning Granny’s comb to see if it is real tortoiseshell: discovering for himself.
evidence: Edmund did not want to learn things: He wanted to find things out, which is quite different.
It was Edmund who cut open the India rubber ball to see what made it bounce,

questions.prompt: The narrator says Edmund skipped school because he was “a kindhearted boy” who did not want to waste the master’s time. Is that the real reason? How can you tell she is joking?
facilitatorNotes: No: he simply did not want to go. She pretends to praise him with a long, solemn excuse that no one would believe; the grand words make the joke.
evidence: He played truant whenever he could, for he was a kindhearted boy,

questions.prompt: Where do other truants go, and where does Edmund go? Why?
facilitatorNotes: They go gathering nuts and berries in the green woods; Edmund goes up the mountain, where people are afraid of the strange noises from the caves, because he wants to find out what makes them.
evidence: He always went up the mountain where the great rocks were,
He wanted to find out what made them.

questions.prompt: Edmund hears three noises in the cave. Describe each one. What might be making them?
facilitatorNotes: A heavy rumble like a large old gentleman asleep after dinner, a smaller rumble, and a clucking like a chicken as big as a haystack. Predictions will vary; the comparisons hint at something huge and sleepy and something like an enormous bird.
evidence: like a very large old gentleman asleep after dinner;
such as a chicken might make if it happened to be as big as a haystack.

readings.title: Kind Little Edmund, part 2: The cockatrice’s fire
readings.challenge: Picture a creature built from many animals, and catch the narrator’s jokes about school.
readings.focus: Edmund rescues a dying cockatrice and is rewarded with stories nobody at school will believe.
readings.context: Recap: Edmund, a boy who would rather find things out than learn them at school, is exploring the caves in the mountain to discover what makes the frightening noises people hear there. He has heard three: a big rumble, a smaller rumble and a giant clucking. A griffin is a creature part eagle, part lion; a cock’s comb is the red crest on a rooster’s head; a snapdragon was a Christmas game of snatching raisins from burning brandy; geological formations are the shapes and layers of rock.
readings.contentNote: Edmund is caned (hit with a stick) by his schoolmaster, a common school punishment in Nesbit’s time. A splash of the cockatrice’s burning fire burns Edmund’s hand.

excerpt.locator: VIII. “Kind Little Edmund,” from the hole in the cave wall to the master’s second caning; opens “"It seems to me," said Edmund to himself, "that the clucking is nearer than the others."…”; closes “…was ignorant and unbelieving: but I am told that some schoolmasters are not like that.”.

questions.prompt: What does the cockatrice look like? Why is it dying?
facilitatorNotes: A man’s face, a griffin’s body, feathery wings, a snake’s tail and a rooster’s comb. Its fire has gone out: it must stir it with its tail once every hundred years, and it overslept.
evidence: This person had a man's face and a griffin's body,
My fire's gone out!

questions.prompt: What does Edmund use to light the fire? What is the joke about the lesson books?
facilitatorNotes: Pine sticks and “a lesson book or two that he had forgotten to lose before.” The joke is that he usually loses his schoolbooks on purpose; for once that habit helps.
evidence: a lesson book or two that he had forgotten to lose before,

questions.prompt: What does Edmund ask for as his reward, and what does the cockatrice tell him?
facilitatorNotes: Stories about “true things that they don’t know at school”: mines, treasure and rocks, but also gnomes, dragons, the unicorn and Magic. The list mixes real science with magic, and Edmund believes all of it.
evidence: About true things that they don't know at school,
and about the unicorn and the phoenix, and about Magic, black and white.

questions.prompt: Why does the master cane Edmund even after he shows his burnt hand? What does the narrator think of the master?
facilitatorNotes: The master decides the story is a lie and the burn is just mischief with fire. The narrator calls him “ignorant and unbelieving.” Readers may notice that the master has a point, which is part of the joke.
evidence: I see you've been playing with fire—into mischief as usual,
The master was ignorant and unbelieving:

readings.title: Kind Little Edmund, part 3: Mrs. D. and the town
readings.challenge: Follow a warning that no one will believe, and notice what the narrator admits about Edmund.
readings.focus: Edmund wakes a dragon, tries to warn the town, and watches the worst happen.
readings.context: Recap: exploring the mountain caves, Edmund found a dying cockatrice, a creature part rooster, part griffin, part snake, and relit its fire. Since then it has told him wonderful stories, but when Edmund tells the schoolmaster, he is caned for lying. Obstinate means stubborn; a centipede is a creature with very many legs; archers shot arrows from holes in town walls; amiable means friendly.
readings.contentNote: Edmund is caned (hit with a stick) by his schoolmaster, a common school punishment in Nesbit’s time. A dragon swallows the whole town, with Edmund’s granny in it.

excerpt.locator: VIII. “Kind Little Edmund,” from the brass passage and the green door to the swallowing of the town; opens “Now, one day Edmund made a new lantern out of something chemical that he sneaked from the…”; closes “…a mouse. Edmund gasped once or twice, and then ran into the cave to tell the cockatrice.”.

questions.prompt: What do the signs on the green door say? Why does Edmund wait before knocking?
facilitatorNotes: “Mrs. D. knock and ring” and “call me at three.” His watch says a quarter to three, so he waits; it still works only because he has not had time to take it apart. The narrator calls the waiting kindhearted.
evidence: call me at three.
he had not yet had time to take it to pieces and see what made it go, so it was still going.

questions.prompt: What does Edmund do when he sees the dragon, and how does the master respond?
facilitatorNotes: He races to school to warn everyone. The master canes him, and when Edmund points to the yellow cloud over the mountain, the master calls it “only a thunder shower.”
evidence: There's a great dragon coming! Somebody ought to do something, or we shall all be destroyed.
It's only a thunder shower,

questions.prompt: What does it mean that the master “would not believe his own eyes”? Why is the sentence he writes on the board funny?
facilitatorNotes: He will not change his mind even when he sees evidence. His sentence, “Lying is very wrong, and liars must be caned,” is aimed at Edmund, who is telling the truth; the one denying the truth is the master.
evidence: would not believe his own eyes if they told him anything different from what he had been saying before his eyes spoke.
Lying is very wrong, and liars must be caned.

questions.prompt: As the dragon comes near, what does Edmund feel about his granny, and about his master? What does the narrator admit?
facilitatorNotes: He grieves for his granny. About the master, the narrator admits Edmund was “not as sorry as he ought to have been” that the master would learn the truth this way. Readers may find that funny, shocking, or very human.
evidence: Oh, my poor, dear granny,
I am afraid he was not as sorry as he ought to have been

readings.title: Kind Little Edmund, part 4: Exactly as he was told
readings.challenge: Follow Edmund’s reasoning about the three noises, and notice how someone finally manages him.
readings.focus: The cockatrice refuses to explain, and for once Edmund does as he is told.
readings.context: Recap: Edmund woke a huge yellow dragon, Mrs. D., and tried to warn his town, but the schoolmaster caned him for lying. From the mountain Edmund watched the dragon swallow the whole town, with his granny in it. Now he has run to his friend the cockatrice, who lives in a basin of fire. A drakling is a baby dragon; Draco centipedis is a made-up Latin name meaning “hundred-footed dragon”; a Baptist chapel is a church building.

excerpt.locator: VIII. “Kind Little Edmund,” from the cockatrice’s “What then?” to Edmund leading the drakling away; opens “"Well," said the cockatrice thoughtfully, when the tale had been told. "What then?"”; closes “…forgotten to be frightened, said, "Come on then," and they went back to the cockatrice.”.

questions.prompt: How does the cockatrice first answer Edmund’s terrible news? Why doesn’t it understand?
facilitatorNotes: “What then?” and “Does it matter?” and “You can live here with me.” It does not know what a granny is. Edmund explains patiently until he loses patience.
evidence: Does it matter?
I don't know what a granny may be,

questions.prompt: When Edmund asks “But why?”, what does the cockatrice do? Why does the narrator call it “exactly the right way to manage Edmund”?
facilitatorNotes: It refuses to explain (“take it or leave it”) and goes to sleep snoring. Edmund, who argues with everyone, respects it at once and obeys, perhaps for the first time. Readers can discuss whether refusing to explain is ever good teaching.
evidence: I give you advice; take it or leave it—
Now this was exactly the right way to manage Edmund, only no one had ever thought of trying to do it before.

questions.prompt: How does Edmund work out where to find the drakling?
facilitatorNotes: From the three noises: the clucking was the cockatrice, the big rumble the dragon, so the smaller rumble must be the drakling. His habit of finding things out is useful after all.
evidence: Of course, the clucking had been the cockatrice,
So the smaller rumbling must have been the drakling.

questions.prompt: What gives Edmund courage at the drakling’s door? What is the drakling like when it wakes?
facilitatorNotes: Remembering the cockatrice’s grim eye and determined snore. The drakling is sleepy and obedient like a small child, insists on its shoes because “Mother said” so, and is “only about the size of a Baptist chapel.”
evidence: he remembered the grim expression of the cockatrice's eye,
Mother said I was never to go out without my shoes,

readings.title: Kind Little Edmund, part 5: The way down
readings.challenge: Follow a two-part trick, and decide whether Edmund is changing.
readings.focus: Edmund and the cockatrice trap the drakling and trick the dragon into giving back the town.
readings.context: Recap: a great dragon has swallowed Edmund’s town, granny and all. His friend the cockatrice, a fiery creature who will not explain its advice, told him to fetch the dragon’s baby, the drakling, which has a hundred feet and wears fifty pairs of copper shoes. Edmund woke it and brought it to the cockatrice’s cave. A shaft is a deep, narrow passage; “done to a turn” means cooked just right; “Facilis descensus” is Latin for “the way down is easy.”
readings.contentNote: Edmund hooks the drakling by its tail to hold it in a shaft.

excerpt.locator: VIII. “Kind Little Edmund,” from the drakling in the cockatrice’s cave to the dragon coughing up the town; opens “The cave was rather narrow for the drakling, but it made itself thin, as you may see a…”; closes “…carefully." And with that he coughed—and choked—and there was the town, on the hillside.”.

questions.prompt: What rule does the cockatrice teach the drakling? Why is it funny coming from the cockatrice?
facilitatorNotes: “We must not ask for all we see,” a nursery rule about manners. A fire-dwelling monster scolding a dragon-baby like a nanny is the joke.
evidence: Did they never teach you that 'we must not ask for all we see'?

questions.prompt: How does Edmund trap the drakling? Why can’t it turn back?
facilitatorNotes: He shows it the way down to the fire in the middle of the earth, and as it goes down he hooks its tail. The way down is easy, but no one can come back up.
evidence: caught the end of the drakling's tail and ran the iron hook through it
the way to the fires below is very easy to go down, but quite impossible to come back on.

questions.prompt: Why does the cockatrice tell Edmund to laugh at the dragon? What does it shout, and what happens?
facilitatorNotes: To bring her to the cave and make her believe she swallowed her own baby with the town. She coughs the town up to search it, and it lands on the hillside.
evidence: You've eaten your own drakling—swallowed it with the town.
And with that he coughed—and choked—and there was the town, on the hillside.

questions.prompt: Edmund obeys “for a wonder” this time. Do you think he is changing? Find evidence.
facilitatorNotes: He almost asks “Why?” and stops himself, does exactly as he is told, and feels “very busy and important.” Some readers will say he is learning; others that he only obeys the cockatrice because he admires it.
evidence: Edmund very nearly said "Why?" but he stopped in time,
doing exactly as he had been told, for a wonder,

readings.title: Kind Little Edmund, part 6: Nobody believes him
readings.challenge: Judge whether the narrator’s praise of Edmund is meant seriously, and notice how the story ends.
readings.focus: Edmund saves the town, and still no one but his granny believes him.
readings.context: Recap: a great dragon swallowed Edmund’s town. On his friend the cockatrice’s advice, Edmund sent her baby, the drakling, down a shaft toward the fire in the middle of the earth, hooking its tail to hold it there, and the cockatrice tricked the dragon into coughing the town back up. A goods train is a freight train; vexatious means annoying; a wild-goose chase is a hopeless search; to be apprenticed is to work for a craftsman while learning a trade.
readings.contentNote: Edmund is caned (hit with a stick) by his schoolmaster, a common school punishment in Nesbit’s time. The dragon and her baby are shut away under the earth for good.

excerpt.locator: VIII. “Kind Little Edmund,” from the trapping of the dragon to the end of the story; opens “Edmund had run back to the cockatrice, and it had told him what to do. So before the…”; closes “But he is quite an old man now, and he hasn't gotten that door open yet!”.

questions.prompt: How does Edmund get the dragon down the hole for good? What does the narrator say about her as a mother?
facilitatorNotes: He pinches the drakling’s tail so it howls; the dragon squeezes into the mountain to find it; he lets the tail go, the baby slides down, and she plunges after it. Then he slams the iron door. The narrator says “she was an excellent mother”: that is exactly what traps her.
evidence: Whatever may have been the poor dragon's other faults, she was an excellent mother.
When the last joint of her tail had gone Edmund slammed down the iron door.

questions.prompt: Edmund is “glad” that the dragons will have plenty to eat forever. Is that kind? What do you think the narrator means?
facilitatorNotes: The narrator calls it kindhearted, but he has shut them under the earth for ever. Many readers hear the narrator joking; others think it really is better than the dragon eating towns. Both can be argued.
evidence: he was glad to think that dragon and drakling would now have plenty to eat of their favorite food, forever and ever.

questions.prompt: How does the master explain away the dragon? What proof does Edmund offer, and why doesn’t it work?
facilitatorNotes: The master calls it a thunderstorm and an earthquake. Edmund points out that the town now stands on the hillside, but the master, the class and even the maps say it always did. Edmund believes the shock changed the maps; no one else does.
evidence: There was a thunderstorm and an earthquake, that's all.
the shock of being swallowed by the dragon had upset all the maps and put them wrong.

questions.prompt: “Only one good thing came of all this long story.” What changed in Edmund? Has he stopped wanting to find things out?
facilitatorNotes: He argues less and becomes a locksmith’s apprentice, but only so he can one day pick the cockatrice’s lock and find out more. He is still curious, even as an old man, and the door is still shut.
evidence: He does not argue quite so much,
so that he might one day be able to pick the lock of the cockatrice's front door
